name: Amazon FBA business
blurb: Buy or make products, ship them to Amazon's warehouses and let Amazon pack and deliver
title: Amazon FBA Business: How It Works, Fees and Risks
description: How an Amazon FBA business makes money, the fees that eat the margin, what you need to start, the course-seller hype to avoid and how to test a product cheaply.
h1: How to start an Amazon FBA business
answer: Amazon FBA (Fulfillment by Amazon) means you source products, send them to Amazon's warehouses, and Amazon stores, packs, ships and handles returns when they sell. You earn the gap between the selling price and what the product, shipping, Amazon's fees and advertising cost you. The catch is that fees, ad spend and unsold stock can quietly swallow the margin, and you are dependent on one platform's rules.

sections.h: How an Amazon FBA business makes money
body: You buy stock (from a manufacturer, a wholesaler or by retail arbitrage), list it on Amazon and keep what is left of each sale after costs. Many sellers build a private-label product: a common item with their own brand, packaging and listing.

At the time of writing, Amazon's US pricing page lists two selling plans: Individual at $0.99 per item sold, or Professional at $39.99 a month. On top of that come a referral fee on each sale (a percentage of the price that varies by category, with a minimum), FBA fulfillment fees based on size and weight, monthly storage fees, and extra fees for inventory stored longer than 181 days. Advertising inside Amazon is optional on paper but most new listings rely on it to be seen.
What usually eats the margin: ads, returns, storage of slow stock, price wars on shared listings and freight.

ul: A seller account, with identity and bank details verified by Amazon.
Money for the first batch of stock, samples, freight and a few months of fees and ads. Stock is the big cost.
A supplier you have vetted with samples, and a way to inspect quality before goods ship.
Product barcodes, packaging and labels that meet Amazon's prep requirements, plus any safety certificates your category needs.

Local paperwork: rules differ by country. Typically a business registration, sales-tax or VAT registration where you sell, and import paperwork if you bring goods in from abroad; check with your tax authority.
Spreadsheet skills to work out landed cost and profit per unit before ordering.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: People comfortable with numbers, suppliers and logistics
Anyone looking for a hands-off side income
Someone who can tie up cash in stock for months
People who would need to borrow to buy the first order
Sellers willing to build a real brand, not copy a listing
Anyone uneasy relying on one platform's rules

ul: Course and coaching sellers: many "FBA blueprints" earn more from students than from selling. Be wary of paid lists of "winning products", since everyone who buys the list competes for the same items.
Account suspension: Amazon can block listings or freeze payouts over complaints, policy breaches or authenticity claims, and appeals take time.
Intellectual property: copying a design, brand or patented feature can get listings removed and lead to legal claims.
Fee changes: Amazon adjusts its fees, and a thin margin can disappear with one update.
Cash-flow traps: money sits in stock and ads for weeks before payouts arrive, and slow stock keeps costing storage.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Pick three product ideas and read the reviews of the top listings for each; look for complaints you could fix.
Order samples from two or three suppliers before committing to a bulk order.
Build a cost sheet per unit: product, freight, referral fee, fulfillment fee, storage, returns and an ad budget.
Check the result against the price the item actually sells for today, not the price you hope for.
Register the business and check the tax registrations you need for the countries you will sell in.
Open the seller account and read the policies for your category before you order stock.
Place a small first order, inspect it and ship it to Amazon following the prep rules.
Write a clear listing with honest photos, then run a modest ad budget and record cost per sale.
Track profit per unit weekly and only reorder once the numbers hold up.

faq.a: No. Amazon handles packing and shipping, but you still source products, manage stock levels, run ads, answer policy issues and handle supplier problems. It can be run part-time, but it is an active retail business.

faq.q: What is the difference between FBA and FBM?
faq.a: With FBA, Amazon stores and ships your stock for a fee. With FBM (fulfilled by merchant) you store and ship orders yourself, avoiding those fees but doing more work.

faq.q: Can I sell other brands' products on Amazon?
faq.a: Sometimes. Some brands and categories are restricted and need approval, and you must be able to prove products are genuine, usually with invoices from an authorised source. Selling counterfeit or unauthorised branded goods risks suspension.
